lesson.title: Where the Parabola Meets the Ground
lesson.summary: Solving a quadratic equation by graphing means finding the x intercepts of its parabola, the points where the curve crosses the x axis and y equals zero.
lesson.body:
A quadratic equation like ax^2 + bx + c = 0 and a quadratic function like y = ax^2 + bx + c are two views of the same object. The equation asks for the specific x values that make the expression equal zero. The function describes a parabola over the whole coordinate plane. A solution to the equation is exactly an x value where the parabola's height, y, is zero, which is precisely where the curve crosses the x axis. This is why solving by graphing works: you draw the parabola using what you already know from graphing quadratics, the vertex, the axis of symmetry, and the general shape, and then you simply read off where the curve touches the horizontal axis.

To solve this way, first put the equation in the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0, then graph y = ax^2 + bx + c. Find the vertex using x = -b / (2a), plot it, then plot a couple of points on each side using symmetry, and sketch the parabola through them. The x coordinates of any points where the curve crosses the x axis are the solutions, often called roots or zeros of the equation.

Consider x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0. The vertex occurs at x = -(-2) / (2 * 1) = 1. Plugging x = 1 into the function gives y = 1 - 2 - 3 = -4, so the vertex is (1, -4), a low point since a = 1 is positive. Testing a few more x values: at x = -1, y = 1 + 2 - 3 = 0, and at x = 3, y = 9 - 6 - 3 = 0. The parabola crosses the x axis at x = -1 and x = 3. Checking both in the original equation confirms it: (-1)^2 - 2(-1) - 3 = 1 + 2 - 3 = 0, and (3)^2 - 2(3) - 3 = 9 - 6 - 3 = 0. Both check out, so the solutions are x = -1 and x = 3.

Not every parabola crosses the x axis twice. Depending on the equation, the graph might cross twice, just touch the axis once at the vertex, or miss the axis completely and stay entirely above or below it. Those three pictures correspond to three very different kinds of answers, and later, when you meet the discriminant, you will see there is a quick algebraic test that tells you which picture you are dealing with before you even draw anything.

Graphing is a genuinely useful way to see what is happening and to estimate solutions, but it has a real limitation: unless the intercepts land on nice grid points, you can only read off approximate values by eye. That is exactly the motivation for the more precise algebraic techniques coming next, solving by square roots, completing the square, and the quadratic formula, all of which give you exact answers every time, whether or not the graph is convenient to draw.
